text.p: British credit and insurance group Provident Financial Plc said on Thursday it had sustained solid growth in the first quarter of 1997 and was confident of continuing the good performance seen in 1996.
"We have every reason to believe that the sort of (growth) trends we have seen will continue," chief executive Howard Bell told Reuters in an interview at the company's annual meeting.
He dismissed analysts' claims that the company could not rely on organic growth from its core home credit loans business.
"We take the opposite view. All our research says there is substantial unsatisfied demand," he said.

Provident, which makes most of its profits from small cash loans to those deemed uncreditworthy by Britain's main banks, increased pre-tax profits from its credit loans business by 20 percent to 111.4 million stg in 1996. Total company pre-tax profits for 1996 were 118.5 million stg, up 17 percent.

Provident said it would continue to generate profit growth from its home credit business through increased revenue. This would be achieved through a larger customer base and more customer agents, Howard said.
And while the company would continue to consider the options of an acquisition and a share buyback scheme, it was in no rush to push these through.
"We believe the existing businesses have good growth prospects," said finance director Robin Ashton.

He said Provident would aim to keep its cost base stable whilst increasing revenue. But he saw little scope for an extension of the cost-cutting programme which, he said, had transformed the company into a profitable organisation in the early 1990s.

Ashton said Provident's insurance business faced lower volumes as the company would maintain its current pricing levels in a competitive market. But he said its refusal to compromise premiums had enabled it to maintain profitability.
Both Bell and Ashton were confident that an incoming Labour government would not pose a threat to Provident's high interest lending.

"There is probably a greater understanding of our business amongst Labour politicians than the Conservatives," said Bell. "They recognise what would happen if we didn't exist. There is a sympathy with our business."
But he was not entirely dismissive of a threat from Labour.

"We take a serious view about any issues that might have an impact positively or negatively on our business. We have good contact with lots of organisations, we explain our business to lots of people."
Provident's executive chairman John van Kuffeler is renowned for his connections and smooth handling of any threats to the business.

Bell also responded to claims made by a recent UK television programme that a loan to one of Provident's customers was at an extortionate rate of interest. "Since that programme he's had another loan from us," he said.
